content: Glutamine is classified as a conditionally essential amino acid, meaning that under certain conditions, such as metabolic stress, the body's natural production of glutamine may not meet the demands of tissues. Research has shown that glutamine supplementation can improve clinical outcomes in critically ill adults. Based on this, it has been hypothesized that glutamine supplementation might also be beneficial for preterm infants. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of glutamine supplementation on mortality and morbidity in preterm infants. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's standard search strategy. This included searches of databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Maternity and Infant Care up to December 2015, as well as conference proceedings and prior reviews. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared glutamine supplementation to no supplementation in preterm infants from birth until hospital discharge. Data were collected and analyzed using the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's standard methods. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. A fixed-effect model was used to synthesize the data, and outcomes were reported as typical relative risk, typical risk difference, and weighted mean difference. A total of 12 randomized controlled trials involving 2877 preterm infants were identified. Six of these trials investigated enteral glutamine supplementation, while the other six examined parenteral glutamine supplementation. The methodological quality of the trials was generally high. However, meta-analysis revealed no significant effect of glutamine supplementation on mortality, with a typical relative risk of 0.97 (95% confidence interval 0.80 to 1.17) and a risk difference of 0.00 (95% confidence interval -0.03 to 0.02). Additionally, there was no evidence of a reduction in major neonatal morbidities, such as invasive infections or necrotizing enterocolitis. Three trials that evaluated neurodevelopmental outcomes in children aged 18 to 24 months and older also found no significant effects of glutamine supplementation on these outcomes. In conclusion, the current evidence from available trials does not support the notion that glutamine supplementation provides significant benefits for preterm infants in terms of reducing mortality, major neonatal morbidities, or improving long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.
